nameStory: This moss earned the name "turgid" from the Latin word meaning "swollen" or "bloated," perfectly describing its plump, puffy appearance. When you see its densely overlapping scales creating that characteristically swollen look, the name makes perfect sense! It's also called "swollen thread-moss" for the same reason - those shoots look like they've been inflated.
description: Turgid Aulacomnium Moss is a rare mountain moss that looks distinctly plump and swollen compared to other mosses. It grows in small cushions or mats, with individual shoots reaching up to 4 inches tall. The densely packed, overlapping scales give the entire plant a puffy, almost inflated appearance that's quite unique among New England mosses. This is definitely a special find - it's been spotted only a handful of times in our region!

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, dense cushions or mats with shoots that look distinctly swollen and puffy, quite different from the typical feathery or flat appearance of most mosses

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels unusually thick and spongy when gently pressed, with a turgid, inflated quality that gives it a balloon-like resilience

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Individual scales are blunt and deeply concave (cupped), about 1/8 inch long, overlapping so densely they create the characteristic swollen appearance

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found only in alkaline conditions on exposed rocky ledges and crags, often in harsh mountain environments where few other mosses thrive

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Typically yellowish-green to pale green, sometimes with a slightly grayish cast, especially when dry

habitat: In New England, this extremely rare moss is found only in harsh alpine and subalpine environments on rocky ledges and cliff faces. It requires alkaline conditions, so look for it on limestone or other calcium-rich rock outcrops at higher elevations. The exposed, windswept locations where it grows are challenging environments that few other plants can tolerate.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as snowmelt provides moisture, and the swollen appearance is most pronounced during this hydrated period.
seasonality.summer: Maintains its characteristic puffy form but may appear slightly more compressed during dry spells, though still distinctly turgid compared to other mosses.
seasonality.fall: Color may shift to more yellowish-green tones, but the diagnostic swollen growth form remains clearly visible.
seasonality.winter: Often buried under snow in its alpine habitat, but when exposed, appears more grayish and compressed, though still noticeably plump.

funFact: This moss was completely wiped out from England in 1878 and has never managed to come back, making the few New England populations incredibly precious survivors of what was once a more widespread species!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the more common ribbed bog moss, but turgid moss has that distinctive swollen, inflated look while ribbed bog moss appears more normal and feathery. Think of it as the difference between a deflated balloon and an inflated one - turgid moss is always "inflated."
contextualKnowledge: With only 4 recorded observations in all of New England, this is one of our rarest mosses and may represent isolated populations clinging to survival in our region's harshest mountain environments.
compareHints: Unlike its relative ribbed bog moss which grows in wet, acidic bogs and has a more typical feathery moss appearance, turgid moss lives on alkaline rocky ledges and has that unmistakable swollen look. Ribbed bog moss also tends to be taller and more loosely arranged, while turgid moss forms tight, puffy cushions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative goose egg moss which prefers drier habitats and forms looser tufts, ribbed bog moss sticks to wet places and forms tighter cushions.
Among its Aulacomnium relatives in New England, goose-egg moss is easily distinguished by its egg-shaped propagule clusters, which the others lack.
Unlike its relative ribbed bog moss which forms dense, tall cushions in sphagnum bogs, bud-headed groove-moss stays much smaller and looser in growth.
